item.title: Man Suspected of Shoving Woman in Front of Bus Is Found Dead, BBC Says
item.description:
A man who had been arrested on suspicion of shoving a woman in front of a moving bus in London in 2017 was found dead at his home on Tuesday, the BBC reported.

The Metropolitan Police said its officers had been called to an address in the West London neighborhood of Chiswick around 7 p.m. Tuesday after a 44-year-old man was found unresponsive at a house there. He was later pronounced dead, the police said, adding that the death was “unexpected but is not believed to be suspicious.”

The police did not name the man, but the BBC and multiple British news outlets identified him as Nicholas Brandram, 44, who was arrested in June in connection with the 2017 attack and had been released on bail. He had not been charged in the case.

According to the BBC, Mr. Brandram’s family said in a statement on Thursday that he “took his own life after months of immense pressure caused by a Metropolitan Police investigation” and there was “no credible evidence” linking him to the incident.

In May 2017, a male jogger, apparently unprovoked, shoved a 33-year-old woman in front of a bus as it was traveling along Putney Bridge in West London.

The woman fell backward and narrowly avoided serious injury when the bus driver abruptly swerved into the next lane, according to CCTV footage of the crime, which shocked Britain.

Surveillance cameras captured the jogger running on the other side of the bridge about 15 minutes later. He ignored the victim when she confronted him, video footage showed.

“The victim was put in extreme danger when she was knocked into the road,” Sgt. Mat Knowles, the investigating officer from the Putney Safer Neighborhoods Team, said in a statement after the attack. “It was only due to the superb quick reactions of the bus driver that she was not hit by the vehicle.”

At the time, the suspect, who came to be identified in the British news as the “Putney pusher,” was described only as a white man in his early to mid-30s, with short brown hair and brown eyes. The police looked into leads involving more than 50 people but said a year later that the trail had gone cold.

Nine years after the attack, the Met police said in June that they had arrested a 44-year-old man on suspicion of grievous bodily harm in relation to the incident. The police said last week that the man had been released. No charges had been brought.

Mr. Brandram was a former soldier in the British Army who more recently worked in private banking, according to the BBC.

item.title: Major Iranian Airline Suspends Several Flights Abroad, Adding to Isolation
item.description:
A major Iranian airline suspended flights to neighboring countries, adding to the country’s isolation caused by sweeping U.S. sanctions and a naval blockade that have sought to cut off Iran from the global economy.

The airline, Iran’s most prominent private carrier, announced the measures on Wednesday, just over a week after the U.S. Treasury Department put restrictions on Iran’s aviation industry intended to severely limit its ability to operate abroad. The new U.S. measures also make it difficult for other countries and non-Iranian companies to work with the Iranian aviation industry, as doing so could be put them at risk of being punished by the U.S. government.

The flight suspensions are likely to further strain many Iranians’ already fraying links with the outside world and add to their hardship, with much of the population feeling squeezed by an American economic pressure campaign.

Mahan Air, one of Iran’s biggest commercial airlines, will stop flying to Oman starting on Thursday and to Turkey starting on Monday, it said in a notification sent to Iranian travel agencies on Wednesday. It did not explain why in detail, saying only that it would stop flights after unspecified decisions by the Turkish and Omani aviation authorities. It did not cite the sanctions.

The suspension of flights comes as a longstanding economic crisis in Iran has been made worse by the war. The U.S. Navy has instituted a blockade of Iran’s southern ports that has curtailed its ability to export oil or import key goods. The Iranian government raised some fuel prices this month because of the financial pressure, increasing the price at the pump for Iranians who were already enduring spiraling inflation and high unemployment.

Last month, the U.S. Treasury announced an “Economic D-Day” that threatened to punish countries and entities that did business with Iran. It said it would target Iran’s trade in gold and cryptocurrency, among other sectors, helping to send the price of Iran’s currency, the rial, to new lows and making imports more expensive.

Mahan Air issued its announcement after the U.S. Treasury Department imposed sweeping sanctions on 27 Iranian airlines and wider restrictions on the sector this month.

The restrictions are part of a broad U.S. campaign to sever Iran’s ability to skirt restrictions on its financial and military sectors, and cut off what it sees as the government’s use of civilian aviation for military ends.

For Iranians who can afford to travel, the airline restrictions add to the list of problems caused by the economic pressure.

“We, the Iranian people, are the ones who are miserable,” said Marzieh, 62, a housewife living in the southwest of the country. Like others who were interviewed for this article, she spoke on condition that her last name not be published, for fear of retribution by the government. “Day by day, we are being pushed further and further toward ruin.”

Speaking before the airline announced that it was suspending flights, she listed what she saw as the likely result of the new measures: fewer international flights, higher prices and more obstacles to those who want to migrate, seek medical treatment or visit family abroad.

The aviation sanctions could also make it harder to maintain American-made planes used by Iranian airlines.

The Treasury suspended licenses that allowed payments to the Iranian government for American aircraft flying over Iran or forced to make emergency landings there; that allowed planes flying to or from Iran to receive some goods or services in the United States; and that allowed the export of goods or services to Iran to ensure the safety of American-made planes. The Treasury said that it would “consider aviation safety-related requests on a case-by-case basis.”

The Treasury also paused a broad license that had allowed American-made civilian aircraft, or civilian aircraft made up of 10 percent or more U.S. parts, to be flown to Iran.

Because the vast majority of the world’s civilian airliner fleet falls into those categories, sanctions experts said, foreign airlines will now have to apply for a license from the U.S. government if they want to maintain their routes into Iran.

The Treasury also sanctioned Emirati and Turkish companies that it said helped Mahan Air purchase three aircraft this summer.

Iran’s aviation sector has been targeted by the United States for years, because of accusations that it has been used to help fund and equip the country’s militant allies in the Middle East.

The U.S. Treasury imposed sanctions on Mahan Air as early as 2011, saying it helped to ferry militants and members of the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps, the most powerful branch of Iran’s military, which the United States has designated as a terrorist organization. Nonetheless, Mahan had been able to procure planes and continue to fly abroad before the new restrictions took effect.

“I’d frame the whole package this way: Treasury is shutting down a general, no-questions-asked permission system that the regime has exploited for years and replacing it with case-by-case licensing,” said Miad Maleki, a former U.S. Treasury official who worked on Iran issues and has urged the Trump administration to more strictly enforce sanctions on Iranian aviation.

Treasury’s actions, he said, come “in the middle of a war in which the regime is firing missiles and drones at the very Gulf cities its planes fly into.”

Iranians inside the country had a variety of reactions to the new sanctions. Some were concerned that the costs would fall mostly on ordinary people, while others observed that many of them cannot afford air travel anyway because of Iran’s deteriorating economy.

Ensieh, 74, a retired teacher who visits her children occasionally in Europe, said that “while these sanctions do have a significant impact on the government, sanctions targeting Iran’s aviation sector cause the greatest harm to Iranian families and society.”

Others, like Masoud, a 39-year-old accountant in Mashhad, in the northeast of the country, blamed Iran’s government for pursuing military and regional policies that spurred U.S. sanctions.

“People are dealing with so many problems that sanctions on airlines — which perhaps are ultimately used by no more than 5 percent of the population — don’t matter that much to people who have long been struggling to make ends meet,” he said.

item.title: The Racial Disparities of Flood Buyouts
item.description:
Next week will be busy in New York. The United Nations General Assembly draws hundreds of world leaders to Manhattan. Climate Week hosts dozens of events across the city. And on Wednesday, Sept. 23, The Times will host our annual Climate Forward live event.

This year will feature an interview with Energy Secretary Chris Wright at a moment of soaring energy costs. We’ll speak about the data center boom with the activist Erin Brockovich; Josh Parker, the head of sustainability at Nvidia; and Gov. Abigail Spanberger of Virginia. And we’ll hear from the chief executives of solar, nuclear, geothermal and deep sea mining companies. Register for the free livestream here.

Disaster relief

By Claire Brown

After a flood, homeowners are often faced with a difficult choice: Rebuild and risk a repeat disaster or move away. The federal government’s efforts to nudge them toward the second option have resulted in more than 43,000 buyouts in recent decades for damaged and at-risk homes, which are destroyed or moved.

But new research has unearthed a troubling racial gap in what homeowners are paid for their properties, which are sold through the Federal Emergency Management Agency’s Hazard Mitigation Grant Program, an initiative that was started in 1988 and is intended to help with long-term disaster recovery and prevent future losses.From 1989 to 2017, buyout compensation for Black homeowners was at least 6 percent lower than it was for white households, according to a new working paper published by the National Bureau of Economic Research that has not yet undergone peer review.

That difference may be part of the reason Black homeowners who received a FEMA buyout tended to move to homes in worse neighborhoods with as much or more flood risk as their previous homes, whereas white homeowners tended to move into better neighborhoods with less flood risk, the paper found.

“There’s nothing in the flood buyout program that’s explicitly racist like there was in government programs in the 1930s and 40s,” said Christopher Timmins, economics professor at the Wisconsin School of Business who worked on the study. “But that doesn’t mean that the way the systems operate don’t lead to those kinds of outcomes.”

FEMA did not immediately respond to a request for comment on the study.

The FEMA buyout process starts with an independent appraiser who calculates the fair market value of a home. If the home has been damaged in a recent flood, they rely on the market value before the disaster, which determines the buyout offer to the homeowner.

Then, the homeowner has three choices: Accept the offer, appeal the price, or refuse to move. It’s not clear which parts of this process contribute to the compensation gap, said Lala Ma, an associate professor of economics at the University of Kentucky who also worked on the paper.

Some of the problem could lie in the broader housing market. For example, researchers have found widespread racial bias in home appraisals.

But Dr. Ma said bias wouldn’t explain the trend in full.

Another possible explanation is the appeal process. It could be that white homeowners tend to appeal their appraisals more often, and that they successfully petition for higher compensation. The researchers did not have data about which homeowners appealed their offers.

Some homeowners may also feel like they can’t say no to an offer, even if it’s for a lower price than they’d like. A 2012 survey of four cities with buyout programs found that a third of the homeowners felt like they had been forced to participate. Previous research has found that FEMA “offers white disaster victims more than people of color, even when the amount of damage is the same,” my colleague Chris Flavelle has reported.

Policymakers have considered expanding buyout programs and purchasing homes before disaster hits. If they don’t fix the payment gap, “these unequal impacts are going to be magnified,” Dr. Ma said.

There are other possibilities that could explain some of the gap the researchers found. Most of the homeowners in the data set were white, and the sample size of Black homeowners was relatively small. Also, in some cases, insurance payouts and other disaster aid are subtracted from buyout purchase offers, and these subtractions are not reported in the figures the researchers used.

The researchers were able to follow the movements of some of the buyout participants as they settled into new neighborhoods. This tracking revealed another divergence.

White sellers tended to move to better neighborhoods with lower flood risks than their prior homes, but Black sellers tended to move to worse neighborhoods that had higher flood risk. (For the purposes of the study, neighborhoods were considered to be “better” or “worse” based on factors like poverty rates, the percentage of renters and single parents, and environmental risk factors like pollution.)

These outcomes seemed to flow from the payment gaps: The lower a Black homeowner’s payment relative to the predicted fair market value of their property, the worse their new neighborhood.

The paper will undergo peer review before it can be published in a journal, a process that could recast or soften some of the findings.

Climate relocation is still a relatively new phenomenon, and policymakers are trying to understand what works and what doesn’t. Still, the research suggests that buyout participants could use more support during the relocation process, Dr. Timmins said.

“What we need to do is think harder about what happens when you give people a pile of money and say, go find a better place to live,” he added.

If you’re not a Times subscriber yet, we have some news: You can now explore all of our coverage free for your first month in The New York Times app. That’s a month to experience The Times like a subscriber and click through all the links in this newsletter without hitting paywalls.You’ll also have access to all of our climate and environment coverage, plus recipes, trusted product reviews and in-depth sports coverage. Download the app now to explore free for your first month — no credit card required.

And if you already subscribe, thank you.

Conservation

In what would be a seismic shift, the Trump administration is quietly moving to strip a core protection of the Endangered Species Act, according to an internal memo obtained by The New York Times.

Under a new interpretation of the law’s language outlined in the memo, the accidental killing or injury of an animal would no longer be considered illegal; only actions specifically intending to target an animal would.

The change would be transformative because, in the United States, the killing of endangered animals almost always happens incidentally, in the course of economic activity. Until now, industries and individuals could be held accountable for those foreseeable deaths and, as a result, they have been incentivized to avoid them. — Catrin Einhorn

Read the full article.

One last thing

In the Maldives, a low-lying archipelago in the Indian Ocean, researchers are doing something remarkable: They’re growing beaches.

The project, born in a lab at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology a decade ago, uses artificial intelligence, satellite and ocean-current data to predict coastal erosion patterns and create submerged structures that harness currents to coax the beach back.The early results from the company, Coastal Assembly, have been promising. “I have seen it,” said Mohamed Nasheed, who served as president of the Maldives from 2008 to 2012. “It actually works.” — Quinn Glabicki

Read the full article.

Because of the war in Iran’s effects on oil supplies, global fossil fuel emissions are set to fall by around 0.5 percent this year, according to a new analysis by Carbon Brief.

A new poll by The Associated Press finds that 53 percent of Americans are extremely or very concerned about the environmental effects of artificial intelligence.

item.title: Comedians Beyond Borders
item.description:
I’m a very German mother. Or so I’m told by my German-British kids. As my daughter explained to friends over brunch, “My dad is very good at telling funny stories. My mum is very good at telling stories about the Nazis.”

What’s a German mother like (apart from someone who obsessively explains German history to her children)? The comedian Laura Ramoso unpacks it here. (She likes fresh air, red wine, sensible footwear and Idris Elba. Small talk and Starbucks? Not so much.) Ramoso, whose impression is based on her own German mother, has everyone in my household in stitches.

But Ramoso’s appeal goes beyond people who have German mothers, or who are German mothers. Today, I’m writing about cross-cultural humor.

In her sketch “My German Mother When We Go To the Beach,” Laura Ramoso’s mother, played by Laura Ramoso, asks her daughter why she has such small breasts. (“It certainly does not run in the family.”) She then volunteers her for a game of volleyball with strangers before expressing incredulity that Laura has cramps. (“You have cramps? I have never had cramps in my life.”)

For my family, the unfiltered Germanic bluntness on display in Ramoso’s clips feels like a private joke. To me, she’s a version of my mother. To my kids, she’s me. But her videos also get millions of views, from people all over the world, and I wanted to understand why.

We’re used to thinking that humor doesn’t translate easily. It doesn’t travel well compared to, say, drama or music. Everyone gets a love story, even with subtitles. A joke that relies on specific cultural codes and implicit references? That’s harder.

But Ramoso and a growing number of comedians, with the help of the internet, are testing that premise. What if we’re in an age where humor increasingly does translate?

An ancient form

Ramoso had her breakthrough during Covid, when stage jobs dried up and she started posting shorts online. The first of her videos that went viral was a series called “My German mother visiting me in Canada.” After that she added more characters to the mix. Her “The Girl Who Just Got Back From (fill in the blank)” series mocks the tourist whose personality changes after a short trip overseas. She also does her Italian dad, as well as Chiara, the maddeningly unhelpful Italian check-in agent. (“You will miss your flight? Send the flight a letter: ‘I miss you, flight.’ ”)

Ramoso’s videos feature different caricatures, but they tend to follow the same format: Ramoso making rapid-fire jokes, underscored by quick cuts.

It turns out that, in both form and content, Ramoso may have been tapping into features that help humor cross borders.

I spoke to Giselinde Kuipers, a Dutch sociologist who studies cross-cultural humor. Some humor has always traveled better, she said. Slapstick, for example, which relies on physicality, not language. Cultural stereotypes are interesting, she said, because almost every culture has them; they’re one of the most ancient forms of humor out there. (The oldest surviving joke book, Kuipers said, is a collection from late antiquity called the Philogelos, or Laughter Lover, in which Roman citizens mock provincial bumpkins.)

Humor based on stereotypes may be universal as a form, but historically it hasn’t traveled well. Stereotypes need to be recognizable to be funny. But the internet and social media have had two effects, Kuipers said. In the same way that American sitcoms have long been exportable because their format has trained the world on how to recognize something “funny” — a contained setting, canned laughter — the video shorts on TikTok and Instagram have their own visual grammar that signals “funny”: fast talk, jerky edits.

At the same time, these platforms have lowered cultural barriers even further, and made stereotypes more recognizable. You no longer have to have your own German mum to watch Ramoso, as her mother, saying “Ach, Laura,” and “You have so many clothes and none of them are good,” and laugh.

Third culture kid comedy

When I saw Ramoso onstage in London, the people watching with me included Brits, Germans and Americans, a Spanish mother-daughter duo, a group of French girlfriends and an Australian couple.

Ramoso feels at home across several cultures. Her German mother, a surgeon, and her Italian father, a builder, met at a hospital in Burundi. She grew up in Cameroon, Azerbaijan, China and Vietnam because her mother worked for the World Health Organization, and now lives in Canada. She’s a third culture kid who had to try out her jokes in international schools.

I asked Ramoso how many of the jokes she makes about her German mum were actually inspired by her German mum.

“Oh, like 99 percent,” she said. “Just the other week she told me out of the blue: ‘I don’t think muffins should ever have been invented.’ And then she added, ‘and that’s just a fact.’ So I write that down.”

Ramoso says she doesn’t do political satire. “I used to feel bad about not being the kind of comedian who makes jokes about politics,” she told me. “But my favorite kind of comedy is observational satire: taking the microscope and looking at human behavior and amplifying it.”

That’s my favorite thing about her comedy too. It’s not polarizing. It’s just a shared laugh about our shared humanity.

Russians begin voting today in the first parliamentary elections since the full-scale invasion of Ukraine, but they are not wondering about the outcome. The vote will be carefully stage-managed and the result is a foregone conclusion: Vladimir Putin’s party will retain its supermajority.

Still, many Russians are worried about what might come next. Rumors of a military mobilization have filled online information spaces and are discussed in cafes, on trains and in smoking areas near offices.

After seizing Yemen’s Red Sea coastline, the Houthi militia appears to have set its sights on two strategic provinces, including Marib, an economic lifeline.

OpenAI disclosed six new instances of “unexpected or concerning” behavior by its A.I. models.

China has stockpiled huge amounts of oil, increasing its geopolitical power as supplies tighten.

U.N. investigators said there were reasonable grounds to conclude that two U.S. airstrikes on Iran in which at least 178 civilians died amounted to war crimes.

As far-right parties are gaining power in Europe, voters in Sweden gave its center-left party an electoral win.

Mexicans say a reservoir near Mexico City is the world’s largest cesspool. My colleague Emiliano Rodríguez Mega visited the site and spoke to residents, many of whom report high levels of cancer. Watch the video.

The most clicked link in your newsletter yesterday was about Papua New Guinea’s rugby obsession.

Merriam-Webster, the oldest dictionary publisher in the U.S., has added the compound noun to its online dictionary, along with nearly 1,400 new entries. It describes the “feelings of anxiety or sadness that arise on Sunday from the knowledge that the weekend is almost over.” Other added words include looksmaxxing, yacht rock and cuffing season.

North Korea’s economy has grown more than 3 percent in each of the past three years. The expansion has been driven by Kim Jong-un’s exploitation of his own people.

My colleagues spoke with dozens of North Korean defectors, human rights investigators and analysts to understand the country’s forced-labor economy, from coal mining and troops fighting for Russia, to exports of wigs and false eyelashes produced in prison camps. Read more about the human cost of North Korea’s economy.

Watch: The documentary “Knife: The Attempted Murder of Salman Rushdie” follows the author’s painful recovery from the 2022 attack.

Level up: Apartment buildings are going beyond gyms and saunas with meditation rooms, on-site child care and other wellness amenities.

Discover: A one-woman play in Hungary based on Kati Marton’s book is being celebrated as a sign of changing times.

Nourish: Are you eating enough fiber?

Lemon possets are creamy, zesty desserts that feel fancier than they actually are. What makes this British classic special is the soft, delicate curd. The key is using full-fat heavy cream.

Where is this cityscape?

Dili, East Timor

Bujumbura, Burundi

Pristina, Kosovo

Juba, South Sudan

Every morning, when our kids leave for school, my husband tells them, “Be kind and try your best.” It’s become a daily ritual, our attempt to remind them to be good people. Will it work? Who knows! But lately, with all this talk about A.I., I’ve begun to see our daily admonition a little differently.

About 15 years ago, I was at a conference where a technologist raised the possibility of machines acting independently of humans. The notion blew my mind. Don’t humans program machines? I asked him, “Don’t we have the power to make them what we want them to be?”

His explanation changed the way I thought about A.I.: Training a machine-learning model is like parenting a child, he said. You can pass your values on; you can teach your child how to behave with incentives and rewards. But you can’t control who your child ultimately turns out to be.

That was a long time ago. We’ve learned a lot about A.I. since then, though we’re still learning about what we can and can’t control. I’ve also learned a lot about parenting. Training an A.I. is not like parenting a child.

But I still find myself thinking there’s something to the metaphor. How do we make teenagers care about their parents, or the world? Call it the teenage alignment problem; their minds are black boxes too. (Of course, we can still unplug the machines, for now. Teenagers, not so much.)

Let me share one other bit of advice I give my kids: “Go to the party!” If there’s a party, a gig, a dinner you’re invited to this weekend, resist the urge to watch TV — go! And in that spirit, I give you “Ain’t Nobody” by the great Chaka Khan, who definitely knows how to have fun.

Have the best weekend! — Katrin

item.title: Trump Moves Ahead With F-35 Jet Sales to Saudi Arabia Despite Intelligence Concerns
item.description:
The State Department said Thursday that the Trump administration was moving forward with the sale of 48 advanced F-35 fighter jets to Saudi Arabia, despite internal reports by U.S. intelligence agencies that China could acquire or steal the warplane’s technology.

The package of the jets and a spare engine, valued at $24.3 billion, “will improve Saudi Arabia’s capability to deter current and future threats by strengthening its homeland defense,” the State Department said in the announcement. The agency also gave formal notification to Congress of the pending sale.

If the production and delivery of the planes is completed, which would take years, Saudi Arabia would be only the second country in the Middle East to have F-35 jets, after Israel.

The State Department made the announcement one day after The New York Times reported on U.S. intelligence concerns on the sales. Internal reports expressing concerns about the possibility of F-35 technology being compromised by China and Saudi Arabia’s military partnership had been circulating among federal agencies and congressional committees.

One detailed report, issued months ago by the Pentagon’s Defense Intelligence Agency, raised questions about whether the Americans and Saudis would be able to secure sites with F-35 technology. It also raised concerns about the access that Chinese military personnel have to Saudi bases and the prevalent use by Saudi Arabia of Chinese technology in telecommunications infrastructure and defense installations.

Last fall, when administration officials were discussing the possibility of the F-35 sale, the D.I.A. compiled a more general internal report that asked tough questions about the growing partnership between China and Saudi Arabia, The Times reported at the time.

For one thing, China has been selling ballistic missiles to Saudi Arabia and helping it learn how to build such missiles.

Despite those concerns, President Trump announced the F-35 sale last November, on the eve of a visit to Washington by Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman, the de facto leader of Saudi Arabia. The crown prince wants to build up the Saudi military, and he had been trying to buy F-35 jets from the United States for years.

The State Department put together the package and sent it to two congressional committees in June to get informal approval for the sale before announcing it. The department did not get nods of approval from all four of the most senior lawmakers on the committees until the middle of this week, U.S. officials said.

Other lawmakers denounced the sale after the department announced Thursday that it was proceeding.

“The Trump administration should not move forward with its proposed sale of F-35 fighter jets to Saudi Arabia when our own intelligence community is warning that it could put the crown jewels of American military technology within reach of the Chinese Communist Party,” said Representative Raja Krishnamoorthi, Democrat of Illinois, who sits on the House Intelligence Committee.

Lawmakers have 30 days to review the sale and, if they oppose it, bring a joint resolution of disapproval. But such a resolution would need the support of two-thirds of both the House and Senate to be able to avoid a possible presidential veto. The House is on recess until November, and the Senate is about to go on recess, so any resolution introduced now would almost certainly not win passage.

The State Department said in a brief statement on Thursday that all defense sales and transfers follow laws and policy guidance that account for “a broad range of political and economic considerations, including protecting the U.S. military’s technological edge.”

Some Israeli officials have raised concerns about the sale, worried that the transaction would erode Israel’s military advantage over nearby Arab nations. Since the 1973 Arab-Israeli war, U.S. policymakers have tried to ensure that Israel maintains its “qualitative military edge” in the region, as mandated by Congress.

The sale could run into pitfalls well before the jets would be delivered or even produced. The Biden administration ended the process for a sale of F-35 jets to the United Arab Emirates that Mr. Trump announced in 2020, near the end of his first term. U.S. intelligence agencies expressed concerns then about the close ties between China and the Emirates.

Saudi Arabia is by far the biggest buyer of American weapons and has relied on them in recent wars. In 2015, Prince Mohammed started a disastrous war against the Houthis in Yemen, one in which Saudi-led forces dropped American-made bombs on civilians. Because of the U.S.-Israeli war against Iran, fighting between the Saudis and the Houthis, who are supported by Iran, has reignited.

Robert Jimison contributed reporting.

item.title: Russia and China Veto U.S. Resolution to Renew U.N. Monitoring of Iran Nuclear Program
item.description:
Russia and China vetoed a U.S. bid to renew the mandate of U.N. experts monitoring nuclear sanctions against Iran at the U.N. Security Council on Thursday. The move deepened tensions between the geopolitical rivals over the Trump administration’s efforts to isolate the Islamic republic.

The nations’ U.N. representatives traded pointed remarks at the Security Council meeting in New York, less than a week before a much-anticipated meeting in Washington between President Xi Jinping of China and President Trump.

Fu Cong, China’s U.N. ambassador, urged Council members to avoid “double standards, political manipulation, pressure and confrontation” at the meeting.

Vasily Nebenzya, Russia’s U.N. ambassador, condemned what he called “the destructive path of our Western colleagues, determined purely by their economic interests in exerting pressure on the Islamic Republic of Iran.”

Iranian officials did not immediately address the vote or the veto.

The clash revolved around a U.S. resolution to extend the work of a panel of experts created to monitor Iran’s nuclear program and its efforts to evade international sanctions. A separate U.N. nuclear watchdog, the International Atomic Energy Agency, reported this month that it had been denied access to Iran’s nuclear facilities.

Britain and France, along with eight nonpermanent members of the Council, voted in favor of the U.S. resolution, with two countries abstaining. But China and Russia, two permanent members of the Council with veto powers, voted down the measure, saying that the sanctions had expired and that the issue should no longer be up for debate. Their representatives also urged a diplomatic end to the U.S. war with Iran and said they supported Tehran’s right to a civilian nuclear program.

Jennifer Locetta, a U.S. ambassador to the United Nations, called the Russian and Chinese vetoes an “act of obstructionism” and said they were aimed at stifling reporting “that implicates their own activities in support of rogue regimes.”

She added that the vetoes would create “a monitoring gap that only benefits the Iranian regime and those who profit from evading those measures.”

In May, U.S. officials said Russia was shipping drone components to Iran via the Caspian Sea, helping Tehran rebuild its offensive abilities amid its war with the United States. Previously, officials also said Russia was providing intelligence to Iran during the war, including satellite imagery showing the locations of warships and military personnel.

The war, which began with U.S.-Israeli strikes in Iran in late February, has opened a new front in the rivalry between China and the United States. Chinese purchases of Iranian oil have helped keep Iran’s economy afloat.

In August, China reacted forcefully after Mr. Trump announced a new and aggressive sanctions campaign against Iran, with Beijing ordering Chinese companies not to comply with the measures.

Mr. Fu said on Thursday that U.S. decisions to pull out of a 2015 nuclear agreement with Iran and to wage war against the nation this year were “at the root of the current crisis.”

Complicating matters for the United States on Thursday, a U.N. fact-finding mission issued a report stating that it had “found reasonable grounds to believe the United States committed a war crime by launching indiscriminate attacks resulting in the loss of life or injury to civilians or damage to civilian objects.” The report cited two U.S. attacks, including a missile strike in February on an Iranian school that killed more than 150 people, mostly children.

U.S. officials acknowledged in March that a preliminary Pentagon investigation had found the United States was at fault for the strikes. The Trump administration has denied that the U.S. military targets civilians, but has not released the findings of the investigation.

The latest confrontation at the U.N. came the day after a high-level meeting between the foreign ministers of China and Iran in Beijing, at a time when Mr. Trump appears to be running out of options on Iran.

Mr. Trump and Mr. Xi are scheduled to meet in Washington next week. Iran is expected to feature prominently in their discussions, along with the potential extension of a U.S.-China trade truce and ways to cooperate on artificial intelligence safety.

item.title: U.S. Strike on Iranian School May Have Been War Crime, U.N. Report Says
item.description:
United Nations investigators said Thursday that there were reasonable grounds to conclude that two U.S. airstrikes on Iran in February in which at least 178 civilians died had been indiscriminate and amounted to war crimes.

The first of the attacks hit the Shajarah Tayyebeh elementary school on Feb. 28 and killed 157 people, including around 123 boys and girls below the age of 13, the investigators said. They cited what they described as credible independent information.

The second strike took place the same day and hit a sports center and nearby residential buildings in the central city of Lamerd. Iranian sources reported that 22 civilians were killed, including five children, the investigators said. They said a “credible organization” reported that close to 170 people were injured, among them children who sustained life-threatening injuries.

The findings were contained in an 18-page report by the U.N.’s Independent International Fact-Finding Mission on Iran and are to be presented to the Human Rights Council in Geneva on Monday.

The report also details abuses it said amounted to crimes against humanity that were committed by the Iranian authorities in their crackdown on government protesters.

Addressing the strike on the elementary school in Minab, a town in southern Iran, the report said: “The mission finds reasonable grounds to believe that the U.S. committed the war crime of launching an indiscriminate attack resulting in loss of life or injury to civilians or damage to civilian objects.”

“The U.S. failed in its obligation to do everything feasible to verify that it was a military objective,” it said.

American officials refused to discuss the findings. “The Department declines to comment on a report conducted by an outside organization,” the Defense Department said in a statement. “Our investigation remains ongoing, and we have nothing to announce at the moment.”

In March, The New York Times reported that an analysis showed that missile fragments purporting to be from the school strike bore the markings of an American cruise missile. The remnants had serial numbers and other details that were consistent with how the Defense Department and its suppliers label munitions. They appeared to be from a U.S.-made Tomahawk cruise missile.

American officials have ascribed the school strike to a targeting error caused by outdated data.

The school was hit during an attack on a nearby Islamic Revolutionary Guards Corps naval complex, but the U.N. investigators said it was clearly identifiable as a school. They also concluded that the site had been “the intended point of impact” and that it had not been hit by an errant strike. They also said it was not collateral damage.

The mission noted that a Defense Department preliminary investigation had acknowledged that the U.S. was probably responsible. The Pentagon has not published the results of its investigation.

“Nobody did that on purpose,” President Trump told journalists in June. “Mistakes are made. War is nasty.”

U.S. forces did appear to have relied on outdated intelligence, but the failure to verify their target “went beyond negligence,” the U.N. report said.

“Rather, the U.S. directed the strikes at the building of the school while being aware of a substantial risk of striking a civilian object and acting recklessly as regards the possibility that this would happen,” it said.

The Lamerd sports center was adjacent to, but visibly separate from, a Guards Corps building, the report said. It said U.S. forces had employed a Precision Strike Missile that dispersed approximately 180,000 tungsten pellets over a wide area.The weapon’s use in a populated civilian area was “reckless as to the likely extent of death or injury,” it said.

The investigators noted that the U.S. military has confirmed use of the Precision Strike Missile in Iran but that it has denied hitting the sports center. U.S. officials say the attack appears more consistent with an Iranian Hoveyzeh cruise missile. The American claim is at variance with evidence, the report said.

The investigators said they had written to the U.S. government requesting information on the airstrikes and meetings with American military officials. They did not receive a response, they said.

In reaching their conclusions, the investigators said they had taken into account public statements by American officials, including Mr. Trump and Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth, that were dismissive of U.S. obligations under international law to distinguish between civilian and military targets.

The investigators said they had also looked into Iran’s brutal treatment of protesters in the period before the United States and Israel launched their war against Iran. In December 2025 and early this year, the report said, the Iranian government engaged in killing of dissidents “on a staggering and unprecedented scale” across all 31 of Iran’s provinces.

The report noted official estimates that 3,038 people had been killed in the violence and some 25,000 injured, many seriously. But the investigators said they strongly believed the real number of people killed and injured was significantly higher.

In the ensuing crackdown, Iranian security forces arrested thousands of people. And since the start of the year, the government has executed at least 58 people on security-related charges, the report said. More than 70 Iranians, including at least five women and three boys, remain at imminent risk of being sentenced to death or executed over the protests, the report said.

Eric Schmitt contributed reporting.

]]>

item.title: Fighting Intensifies in Yemen as Militia Advances on Key Provinces
item.description:
Fighting has intensified near two strategic provinces in Yemen, a sign that Iranian-backed Houthi militants are expanding their offensive after seizing the country’s Red Sea coastline, analysts say.

A sustained Houthi push into Yemen’s resource-rich eastern regions, including Marib Province, would threaten the economic lifeline of the internationally recognized government and risk triggering a fresh humanitarian crisis among millions of Yemenis.

While the Houthis have succeeded in taking much of northwestern Yemen since capturing the capital, Sanaa, in 2014, Marib has so far eluded them.

“It is the bastion and stronghold in the north for those who resisted the militia’s coup more than a decade ago,” said Mohammed al-Basha, a Washington-based risk analyst focused on Yemen. “If they capture it, it would be such a symbolic and strategic win for them.”

Marib, about 75 miles east of Sanaa, and the southern city of Taiz have emerged as the Houthis’ most likely targets after they captured territory near the Bab al-Mandab Strait, a vital waterway for global trade. That advance has allowed the militia to increase its pressure on shipping in the Red Sea.

Pro-government forces have struck Houthi positions in both provinces with fighter jets and drones over the past month and say they have repelled the militia’s advances. The Houthis have countered by firing missiles at government-held areas.

The Yemeni government has been backed for more than a decade by Saudi Arabia, which has led a military coalition aiming to roll back the militia. The coalition carried out a devastating bombing campaign, but it ultimately failed to oust the Houthis from power.

Since then, Yemen has effectively been divided into two states, with the Houthis in control of large swaths of the country’s north and the government in the south, based in the temporary capital, Aden.

Marib is home to some of Yemen’s largest oil and gas fields. Its loss would deal a severe blow to the government’s finances as well as its claim to legitimacy. Marib’s fall would also open a route for the Houthis toward the eastern province of Hadramout, Yemen’s largest, which shares a long border with Saudi Arabia.

“If Marib falls to the Houthis, it would mean the militia would be in reaching distance to the Saudi-Yemeni borders,” said Ahmed Nagi, a senior analyst for Yemen at the International Crisis Group. “That would be unacceptable to Saudi Arabia and threatens their national security.”

A Houthi political official, Mohammed al-Bukhaiti, said that tribal elders in Marib had called on the group to “liberate” the province. “Sanaa assures everyone that it is committed to liberating every inch of Yemeni territory,” he said in a phone interview. He said Saudi-backed forces had rejected de-escalation efforts.

Yemeni government officials and analysts describe the recent clashes as among the most intense since 2021, when the Houthis last mounted a major assault on Marib but were pushed back. The Yemeni government and Saudi Arabia both appear to be stepping up airstrikes to blunt Houthi advances, said April Alley, a senior fellow at The Washington Institute, where her research focuses on Yemen and the Gulf.

But she said: “The Houthis have the wind at their back for the moment. Government forces are deeply fragmented, and morale took a huge hit after the west coast losses.”

The Houthis said on Wednesday they had shot down a Saudi F-15 fighter jet over Marib with a locally made missile. The wreckage of the downed jet seems to be consistent with that of the F-15 jets in the Royal Saudi Air Force, a review of the images by The New York Times found. However, the exact location of the wreckage could not be confirmed.

In recent weeks, the battlefront has also extended to Taiz, which connects the Houthi-controlled north with the southern coast controlled by the government.

“What the Houthis are doing is trying to besiege the city of Taiz and choke off the last highway connecting Taiz with Aden,” Mr. Nagi said. “Who controls the city would matter strategically for both sides.”

The Houthi-run Saba news agency reported Saudi airstrikes on Thursday in the city of Abs in Yemen’s Hajjah Province that left one person dead and another wounded. The agency said that Saudi aircraft also targeted three telecommunications towers in Taiz Province. A Houthi military spokesperson, Yahya Saree, said that the Saudis had carried out 37 airstrikes using F-15 jets targeting Taiz and Hajjah over the past 24 hours.

Saudi Arabia’s Civil Defense on Thursday said a Yemeni resident had been killed in the Saudi province of Taif, east of Islam’s holiest site, Mecca. They were hit by shrapnel from an intercepted Houthi drone, the Saudis said.

It was the first announced death in the kingdom since the Houthis intensified their cross-border strikes this month. A Pakistani man was injured and in critical condition, the authorities said.

Shuaib Almosawa Almosawa reported from Sanaa, Yemen.

]]>

item.title: Rejecting Trump, South Korean Leader Says He Will Not Send Troops to Iran
item.description:
President Lee Jae​ Myung of South Korea pushed back against pressure from the Trump administration on Friday, declaring that his country would not deploy troops or military assets to support the U.S.-led war against Iran.

In recent weeks, President Trump has publicly taunted the South Korean leader, venting frustration over ​what he described as Seoul’s refusal to help defend the Strait of Hormuz — once the world’s main transit point for oil — while American troops remain stationed on​ ​the Korean Peninsula to shield ​South Korea from North Korea.​ On Friday, Mr. Lee ​firmly rejected any ​military involvement in the Middle East conflict.

“There will be no deployment of troops or dispatch of military assets to​ be involved in or intervene in this war,” Mr. Lee said in a news conference.

Instead of a combat deployment, Mr. Lee noted that Seoul is considering expanding the operational scope of a South Korean navy destroyer and its support ships currently stationed off the coast of Somalia for antipiracy operations. He emphasized that even if those assets move closer to the Red Sea or the Strait of Hormuz, their sole focus would be protecting South Korean ​oil tankers and other commercial vessels. They will not participate in any operations that could be interpreted as supporting the war against Iran​, he said.

​While Mr. Trump has not specified the exact type of assistance he expects from Seoul, he complained last month that he had asked Mr. Lee “to give us a little hand” in the conflict, reminding him of the U.S. military presence in South Korea.

“He said, ‘No, thanks,’” Mr. Trump ​recalled. “I see. Well, why are we involved in helping you?”

It was not the only issue that a grim-faced Mr. Lee addressed on Friday. Fifteen months into his single five-year term, his approval rating has fallen to a new low of 37 percent, battered by troubles brewing not only at home but also by strains with South Korea’s most important ally, the United States.

Last month, Mr. Trump unilaterally scaled down one of the United States’ annual joint military exercises with South Korea, calling the drills not only “costly” but also “totally inappropriate and hostile” toward North Korea. He said that, for as long as he had been in office, North Korea had been “unthreatening and respectful.” Mr. Trump also boasted of having a “very good relationship” with North Korea’s leader, Kim Jong-un, even as the North has become a bigger nuclear threat against the South.

At home, South Korea’s main stock index — once lauded as a premier beneficiary of the global A.I. boom — has crashed, devastating the portfolios of millions of individual investors who were encouraged by Mr. Lee’s government to buy stocks. Mr. Lee has also failed to deliver on his repeated pledges to curb rising housing costs.

The opposition has accused him of seeking a constitutional amendment that would allow him to run for a second term, a move explicitly barred by the current Constitution. His presidency also remains marred by his suspended criminal trials on charges including violating election laws and inducing perjury. The opposition has claimed that Mr. Lee was plotting a special bill to erase those charges, ​which he has insisted were fabrications orchestrated by his conservative adversary and predecessor, the impeached and ousted former President Yoon Suk Yeol.

On Friday, Mr. Lee said that although he supported a constitutional revision allowing future presidents to seek a second term, he himself had no intention of seeking re-election. He called it “constitutionally impossible​.” The claim that he might ​seek a second term, he said, was nothing more than a “political offensive.”

Mr. Lee also said he supported the National Assembly’s appointment of a special prosecutor to investigate whether politicians like him, as well as journalists, had been targeted in politically motivated criminal investigations under Mr. Yoon. But he said that he did not want such a special prosecutor to have the power to drop the criminal charges already filed against him.

“It’s because of my own shortcomings,” Mr. Lee said, referring to his plummeting approval ratings. “I fell short in consideration, sensitivity and communication.”

Mr. Lee also said his government remained in “fierce” negotiations with Washington over how to implement the sweeping agreement the two governments announced last November. Under the pact, Mr. Trump reduced tariffs on key South Korean exports, including automobiles, from 25 percent to 15 percent. He also pledged U.S. support for South Korea’s efforts to develop nuclear-powered submarines and to enrich uranium for civilian nuclear energy. In exchange, Mr. Lee committed $350 billion in investments in the United States.

But negotiations over the deal’s implementation have stalled over the details, fueling doubts on both sides about the other’s willingness to follow through.

On Friday, Mr. Lee said the two governments were close to finalizing an agreement on where the first batch of South Korean investments should go.

Mr. Lee said he had been unhappy with a proposed agreement and had instructed his government to continue negotiating. He did not elaborate, but emphasized that any investment projects must be “commercially reasonable” and that the two governments needed to agree on how to share profits and losses from such projects.

“We should not buckle under pressure or coercion,” he said, adding that his comment reflected his government’s general negotiating principle and was not aimed at the Trump administration in particular.

But Mr. Trump’s complaints that he has received “very little help from other countries” for the war in Iran have placed immense diplomatic pressure on Seoul. The United States led the United Nations forces that repelled North Korean invaders during the 1950-53 Korean War, anchoring what is now a seven-decade-long alliance. South Korean troops formed the largest foreign contingent fighting alongside American forces in the Vietnam War.

Yet, acceding to Mr. Trump’s request would carry severe political risks for Mr. Lee. The last time South Korea sent forces to a U.S.-led conflict — the Iraq War, which began in 2003 — the progressive administration of then-President Roh Moo-hyun faced a fierce domestic backlash, particularly from his own party and base. Although that deployment consisted primarily of engineering and medical units, the decision permanently crippled Mr. Roh’s approval ratings.

Public opinion in South Korea remains against intervention. A poll conducted this month showed that 55 percent of South Koreans oppose deploying troops to the conflict with Iran, compared to just 32 percent in favor.

]]>

item.title: Warnings Across the Himalayas After Nepal Floods
item.description:
It’s not just Nepal.

Glaciers are melting across much of the Himalayas. Long-frozen ground, known as permafrost, is thawing. And a raft of disasters is menacing tens of millions of people who live in the countries that span the world’s highest mountains: landslides, bursting lakes, swollen rivers so forceful they wash away entire communities.

Now, three weeks after a glacier collapsed, unleashing flash floods that left more than 8,000 dead or missing in Nepal and China, experts are urging national and local leaders across the region to prepare better for the next catastrophe. That includes more robust monitoring of their shared mountains and rivers, exchanging data with each other, and putting in place early warning systems and evacuation plans.

“We need a lot more data-sharing and communications across these national borders,” said Miriam Jackson, who studies Earth’s frozen parts, or the cryosphere, as a research scientist for the Norwegian government.

“We are going to see more and more of these events,” she added. “The cryosphere is changing very quickly. We have more and more people living quite close to these hazards. And we need more knowledge.”

Her call was echoed by a report published this week by an environmental consultancy called Systemiq. It found that of 40,000 glaciers in the Hindu Kush Himalayan range, only 21 are being actively monitored. The range spans Afghanistan, Bangladesh, Bhutan, China, India, Myanmar, Nepal and Pakistan.

That is all the more worrisome, scientists say, because the Himalayas, a source of water for two billion people downstream, are being pummeled by climate change. A report issued by scientists this week concluded that fossil fuel emissions played a “very strong” role in the Aug. 26 disaster in Nepal and Tibet, as rising temperatures likely destabilized permafrost and ice under the mountain slopes, leading to the catastrophic flood.

A 2023 report that Dr. Jackson coauthored while she was at the International Centre for Integrated Mountain Development found that glaciers melted 65 percent faster from 2010 to 2019 than in the decade before. An earlier report from the same institute found that even if the global average temperature increase compared to preindustrial levels is capped at 1.5 degrees Celsius — the target limit set as part of the 2015 Paris climate agreement — one-third of the glaciers of the Hindu Kush Himalayas would be gone by the end of this century. In early September, scientists said the world breached that 1.5 degree threshold.

In India alone, nearly 200 glacial lakes are considered to be at high ⁠risk of bursting their banks and 56 at very high risk, according to the Systemiq report. The Indian state of Uttarakhand suffered a similar but smaller-scale rock avalanche struck in 2021, and a glacial lake burst in the Indian state of Sikkim in 2023. Arushi Chopra, one of the authors of the Systemiq report, said there will be others. “It’s not a question of if, but when,” she said.

Several scientists cautioned that while it is unrealistic and even unnecessary to monitor every Himalayan glacier, it’s important to keep an eye on the most at-risk areas, including the glaciers that sit above hydropower dams or large towns and villages, for which a small disturbance in the mountains can have catastrophic consequences.

To focus monitoring efforts on those hot spots would be more viable, said Walter Immerzeel, a mountain hydrologist at Utrecht University in the Netherlands. That would require satellite data keeping an eye on the glacier as a whole, sensors in the ground to measure rock movement and a remote sensing technique called radar interferometry that can provide some early warning for instability in the mountains, avalanches and glacial lake outbursts.

“You cannot monitor every glacier and rock wall in the Himalayas,” he said at an online briefing for journalists Wednesday.

The terrain makes it difficult to install measuring instruments. It’s also exceedingly expensive, especially for countries like Nepal, with limited resources.

Madhab Uprety, a technical adviser at the Red Cross Red Crescent Climate Center, based in Kathmandu, said he hoped this disaster would “open some opportunities” for cross-border monitoring. Because even in a country like Nepal, which has dealt with many floods and landslides in its history, the events of Aug. 26 were unprecedented. “There was no existing monitoring or any warning arrangements to detect it or communicate it at that scale,” Mr. Uprety said.

Cross-border data sharing is further complicated by geopolitical tensions in the region, with several countries in the region having fought wars and disputed borders.

“There’s an urgent need for having greater cooperation among all these Himalayan states,” said Devendra Kumar Sharma, who managed several hydropower dams on Himalayan rivers and who is now president of the International Commission on Large Dams. “Climate change is happening. It doesn’t recognize boundaries.”

Dr. Jackson, the researcher, was in a meeting with other cryosphere scientists when the Nepal flooding unfolded. They all realized early on how awful it would be; they had been warning of something like this for years.

“You know there’s a good chance of this happening,” Dr. Jackson said. “You don’t know when.”

item.title: Why Russia Holds Elections, and How the Kremlin Gets the Results It Wants
item.description:
Russians began voting on Friday in the first parliamentary elections since the full-scale invasion of Ukraine, an exercise carefully engineered by the Kremlin to project popular support for continuing a war now in its fifth year.

Since 2021, when the previous State Duma election was held, the country has changed significantly. The political system has shed its last vestiges of tolerance for dissent. Hundreds of thousands of people have fled the country, including most of its vocal opposition leaders and activists. Almost all antigovernment media outlets have been forced to shut down or operate from abroad.

In recent months, anxiety has been building in society over intensifying economic and political fallout from the war. But the stage-managed election offers little outlet for discontent. According to polls and analysts, the vote is likely to leave the Duma’s composition largely unchanged. The pro-Kremlin United Russia party is expected to retain its legislative supermajority, with four nominal opposition parties splitting the remaining seats.

Here’s what to know about why an authoritarian Russia continues to hold elections and what it does to achieve its desired outcome.

In Moscow, it has been hard to tell that a major election is even taking place. Campaign posters have been scarce, and only a handful of activists have handed out leaflets on streets. There were no large-scale outdoor rallies, and televised debates drew attention only for how uninspired and inarticulate the candidates appeared. On many occasions, candidates skipped the debates altogether.

Still, the voting is critical for those in power, said Ilya Grashchenkov, a political analyst in Moscow who advises Russian politicians and parties.

Mr. Grashchenkov said that stage-managed elections provided the Kremlin with its “sole source of legitimacy.” The government can hold up the results as proof that it is delivering for the Russian people, even with the obvious caveats that come with an unfree vote.

The election also bolsters an official narrative. President Vladimir V. Putin has repeatedly pointed out that Russia continues to hold elections despite the war in Ukraine, contrasting this with Ukraine’s postponement of elections under martial law. (The questionable value of Russian elections, of course, goes unmentioned.)

“We have to stand for election, not be afraid to run for office,” Mr. Putin said in June. “And I would advise everyone to do the same. Especially in Ukraine.”

Elections in Russia are orchestrated through an elaborate, multilayered system managed by the Kremlin’s political apparatus.

First, unwanted candidates are filtered out early. This year, the primary example was the removal from the ballot of the liberal Yabloko party, which has explicitly called for an immediate cease-fire in Ukraine. The party was barred after it rapidly galvanized pro-peace sentiment in Russia, which appeared to be stronger than the Kremlin had expected.

Second, the central government’s political managers set targets for the final composition of the Duma, Mr. Grashchenkov, the political analyst, said. These goals are handed down to regional authorities, who are tasked with delivering specific margins based on their region’s demographic and cultural profiles.

The governors and their political advisers then apply pressure intended to get public sector workers to go to the polls in support of the government. Local companies and businesses that back the government also push workers to cast ballots by entering voters into lotteries or offering other incentives. Because of sparse campaigning in Russia, people who might support opposition candidates feel discouraged from participating in the election.

Finally, the Kremlin uses online voting, which is available in more than a third of Russia’s regions, to fine-tune the result, Mr. Grashchenkov said. While the government is not believed to engage in wholesale rigging of voting results, opposition activists have accused it of altering numbers from online voting, which is easier to do than with paper balloting.

After emerging from the collapse of the Soviet Union in 1991, Russia initially tried to conduct open parliamentary elections modeled on Western systems.

That period was short-lived. In 1993, during the first post-Soviet parliamentary vote, a nationalist party finished first over pro-Kremlin forces. “At that point, the idea emerged that everything needed to be moderated and managed,” Mr. Grashchenkov said.

The intensity of the management has grown steadily over time. In the beginning, the Kremlin leaned on Russian oligarchs to fund pro-government parties. In the 2000s, political strategists were dispatched to the regions to engineer the desired outcomes. In the decade preceding the war in Ukraine, the authorities relied on more heavy-handed tactics, coercing state employees to vote.

After the 2022 invasion, pressure to back the government intensified. The message, Mr. Grashchenkov said, was, “If you’re not with us, you’re against us.”

On Wednesday, in an address before the election, Mr. Putin made it clear that voters should have no second thoughts about whether the war should continue until complete victory.

“Your choice and resolve will show once again that millions of people stand behind our fighters,” Mr. Putin said. “Participating in the elections is our shared contribution to Russia’s victory.”
